note: Original passages. Steps are practice steps ordered by text length and sentence complexity; they are not Lexile measures, grade levels or WIDA levels.

passages.title: Mina's Bike
passages.text: Mina has a red bike. The bike has a loud bell. Every morning, Mina rides to school with her brother. They park the bikes by the gate. After school, they ride home slowly because the road is busy.

questions.q: What color is Mina's bike?
choices: Red
Blue
Green
questions.hint: Look at the first sentence.
questions.why: The first sentence says, "Mina has a red bike."

questions.q: Who rides to school with Mina?
choices: Her teacher
Her brother
Her neighbor
questions.hint: Find the sentence that says "with".
questions.why: The text says Mina rides to school with her brother.

questions.q: Why do they ride home slowly?
choices: They are very tired.
The bell is too loud.
The road is busy.
questions.hint: Look for the word "because" in the last sentence.
questions.why: "Because" introduces the reason: the road is busy.

passages.title: Rain Day
passages.text: It rains on Monday. The children cannot play outside. They stay in the classroom and read books. Sam reads about frogs. Lila draws a picture of the rain. At lunch, the sun comes out.

questions.q: Where do the children stay?
choices: In the classroom
On the playground
In the library
questions.hint: Find the sentence that starts with "They stay".
questions.why: They stay in the classroom and read books.

questions.q: What does Lila do?
choices: She reads a book about frogs.
She draws a picture of the rain.
She plays a game outside.
questions.hint: Find Lila's name in the text.
questions.why: The text says Lila draws a picture of the rain.

questions.q: What is this text mostly about?
choices: A trip to the zoo
A birthday lunch
A rainy day at school
questions.hint: Think about what happens in every sentence.
questions.why: Every sentence is about the rain and what the children do inside.

passages.title: The Sleepy Cat
passages.text: Our cat, Pepper, sleeps a lot. She sleeps on the sofa in the morning. In the afternoon, she sleeps in a sunny spot by the window. At night, she wakes up and plays with a ball. Pepper is a busy cat at night!

questions.q: Where does Pepper sleep in the afternoon?
choices: By the window
On the sofa
Under the bed
questions.hint: Read the sentence that starts with "In the afternoon".
questions.why: In the afternoon she sleeps in a sunny spot by the window.

questions.q: In this text, a "sunny spot" is...
choices: a place that is dark and quiet
a place where the sun shines in
a place that is cold and wet
questions.hint: Think about the window and the sun.
questions.why: A sunny spot is a place that gets light from the sun.

questions.q: When is Pepper most active?
choices: In the morning
In the afternoon
At night
questions.hint: Find the sentence about playing with a ball.
questions.why: She plays with a ball at night, so night is her busy time.

passages.title: Making Lemonade
passages.text: Ana and her cousin wanted to earn money for a new soccer ball, so they made a lemonade stand. First, they squeezed ten lemons and added sugar and cold water. Then they painted a sign with big yellow letters. By noon, they had sold twelve cups. Ana smiled and counted the coins. "We need a few more customers," she said, "but we are close!"

questions.q: Why did Ana and her cousin make a lemonade stand?
choices: They wanted to earn money for a soccer ball.
They wanted to give lemonade to neighbors.
They wanted to win a school prize.
questions.hint: Read the first sentence. Look for the word "so".
questions.why: The first sentence gives the reason: money for a new soccer ball.

questions.q: What did they do right after they made the lemonade?
choices: They sold twelve cups.
They painted a sign.
They counted the coins.
questions.hint: Find the sentence that starts with "Then".
questions.why: "Then they painted a sign" comes right after making the lemonade.

questions.q: What can you tell about Ana at the end?
choices: She is ready to give up and go home soon.
She is upset because the sign is the color yellow.
She thinks they will reach their goal soon.
questions.hint: Read what Ana says: "but we are close!"
questions.why: Ana says they are close, so she expects to reach the goal.

passages.title: Why Leaves Change Color
passages.text: In the fall, many leaves change from green to red, orange, and yellow. Leaves are green because they hold a substance called chlorophyll. Trees use it to make food from sunlight. When the days get shorter, trees make less chlorophyll. The green fades, and the other colors, which were hidden all summer, appear.

questions.q: What is this text mostly about?
choices: Why leaves change color in the fall
How trees grow new roots deep into the ground
Why summer days are so much longer than winter days
questions.hint: Ask: what does the whole text explain?
questions.why: The text explains how chlorophyll and shorter days change leaf color.

questions.q: Why are leaves green in summer?
choices: They get too much water.
They hold chlorophyll.
They are very young.
questions.hint: Find the sentence with the word "because".
questions.why: Leaves are green because they hold chlorophyll.

questions.q: In this text, "hidden" means...
choices: very bright
falling down
not easy to see
questions.hint: The colors were there all summer, but nobody saw them.
questions.why: Hidden colors are there, but you cannot see them yet.

passages.title: The New Student
passages.text: On Tuesday, a new student named Omar joined our class. He spoke quietly and held his backpack tightly. At recess, I invited him to play tag. At first he shook his head, but then he smiled and ran with us. After school, he waved and said, "See you tomorrow!" I think he feels more comfortable now.

questions.q: What did the speaker invite Omar to do?
choices: Play tag
Read a book
Eat lunch
questions.hint: Find the sentence that starts with "At recess".
questions.why: At recess, the speaker invited him to play tag.

questions.q: How did Omar probably feel at the start of the day?
choices: Loud and excited
Shy and nervous
Bored and sleepy
questions.hint: Think about how he spoke and how he held his backpack.
questions.why: Speaking quietly and holding a backpack tightly show a shy, nervous student.

questions.q: In this text, "comfortable" means...
choices: tired and slow
angry and upset
relaxed and at ease
questions.hint: Omar smiled, ran, and waved. How does he feel?
questions.why: A student who smiles and says "See you tomorrow" feels at ease.

passages.title: Life in a Tide Pool
passages.text: When the ocean tide goes out, small pools of seawater stay trapped among the rocks. These tide pools are home to crabs, sea stars, and snails. Animals that live there must survive difficult changes. At low tide, the sun heats the water, and it becomes salty. At high tide, strong waves crash over the rocks. Many animals have hard shells or strong arms that hold on tightly, which helps them stay safe in both conditions.

questions.q: What stays among the rocks when the tide goes out?
choices: Small pools of seawater
A few large fishing boats
Piles of dry sand and shells
questions.hint: Read the first sentence.
questions.why: The first sentence says small pools of seawater stay trapped among the rocks.

questions.q: In this text, "trapped" means...
choices: washed far out to the open sea
caught and unable to leave
slowly warmed by the afternoon sun
questions.hint: The water stays among the rocks when the tide goes out.
questions.why: The water cannot flow back to the ocean, so it is trapped.

questions.q: What problem do tide pool animals face?
choices: They cannot find enough food or fresh water among the rocks.
They live too far away from the ocean to feel the tide.
Their home changes between hot, salty water and crashing waves.
questions.hint: Read the sentences about low tide and high tide.
questions.why: The text describes two difficult conditions: heat and salt at low tide, waves at high tide.

passages.title: The Broken Window
passages.text: While practicing baseball in the backyard, Marcus hit the ball too hard and heard a loud crash. The ball had broken his neighbor's window. His heart pounded. He could run inside and pretend nothing happened, but that did not feel right. Slowly, he walked to Mrs. Lopez's door and knocked. "I'm sorry," he said. "I will use my savings to fix it." Mrs. Lopez thanked him for his honesty and said that accidents happen.

questions.q: What did Marcus decide to do?
choices: Tell Mrs. Lopez and offer to pay
Hide the ball and say nothing
Ask a friend to pay for the window
questions.hint: Find what Marcus says at Mrs. Lopez's door.
questions.why: He apologized and offered to use his savings to fix the window.

questions.q: Which words best describe Marcus?
choices: Careless and rude
Honest and responsible
Lazy and silly
questions.hint: Think about what he chose to do even though it was hard.
questions.why: Telling the truth and offering to pay show honesty and responsibility.

questions.q: What lesson does this story teach?
choices: Baseball is too dangerous to play near houses.
Neighbors should never let children play outside.
Telling the truth is right, even when it is hard.
questions.hint: Look at the sentence "that did not feel right" and Mrs. Lopez's answer.
questions.why: Marcus chose honesty and Mrs. Lopez thanked him for it.

passages.title: The Library on Wheels
passages.text: In some rural areas, people live far from a library. To help them, some communities send a bookmobile, which is a bus filled with books. The bookmobile visits villages on a schedule, so families know when to come. Children borrow picture books, and adults borrow novels and cookbooks. Some buses also offer free internet. For many families, the bookmobile is the only way to reach books.

questions.q: What is a bookmobile?
choices: A bus filled with books
A small library building
A book club for adults
questions.hint: Find the word "which" in the second sentence.
questions.why: The text says a bookmobile is a bus filled with books.

questions.q: Why does the bookmobile follow a schedule?
choices: So drivers can save money on gas
So families know when to come
So the books stay clean and dry
questions.hint: Look for the word "so" in the third sentence.
questions.why: A schedule lets families know when the bus will visit.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Children in villages like picture books better than novels do.
Libraries in many small villages are closing for good.
Bookmobiles bring books to people who live far from libraries.
questions.hint: Choose the idea that covers the whole text.
questions.why: Every detail shows how the bookmobile brings books to far-away families.

passages.title: The Waggle Dance
passages.text: Honeybees cannot talk, yet they can tell each other exactly where to find food. When a worker bee discovers a field of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a "waggle dance." She moves in a figure-eight pattern and shakes her body in the middle. The angle of the dance shows the direction of the flowers compared with the sun, while the length of the shaking shows how far away they are. Other workers watch closely, then fly out to collect nectar. Scientists have studied this dance for decades because it is one of the few examples of animals sharing detailed information.

questions.q: What does the length of the shaking show?
choices: How far away the flowers are
Which flowers have the most nectar
How many bees should go
questions.hint: Find the sentence about "the length of the shaking".
questions.why: The length of the shaking shows how far away the flowers are.

questions.q: In this text, "performs" means...
choices: hides from the other bees
does a set of movements
carries heavy loads of nectar
questions.hint: The bee moves in a figure-eight pattern.
questions.why: Performing a dance means doing its movements.

questions.q: Why do the other workers watch the dance closely?
choices: They want to learn how to talk to the bees.
They are afraid of the bee that is dancing.
They need the information to find the flowers.
questions.hint: Read what the other workers do next.
questions.why: After watching, they fly out to collect nectar, so they used the dance to find it.

passages.title: The Silent Clock Tower
passages.text: In the town of Alder Creek, the old clock tower had been silent for years. Residents argued about whether to repair it or tear it down. Twelve-year-old Priya, who loved gears and springs, volunteered to inspect it. After climbing the dusty stairs, she discovered that a single bent gear had stopped the mechanism. With help from the town's retired watchmaker, she straightened it. At noon, the bells rang for the first time in years, and the crowd below cheered. Priya realized that patience and teamwork had solved a problem others thought was hopeless.

questions.q: What had stopped the clock?
choices: A single bent gear
A broken bell
A missing spring
questions.hint: Find what Priya discovered after climbing the stairs.
questions.why: She discovered that a single bent gear had stopped the mechanism.

questions.q: In this text, "hopeless" means...
choices: very easy to understand and explain
having no chance of being fixed
needing a lot of money to finish
questions.hint: Others thought the problem could not be solved.
questions.why: A hopeless problem seems impossible to fix.

questions.q: Which theme fits the story best?
choices: Old buildings in a town are better torn down than repaired.
Young people should never be allowed to climb tall towers.
Patience and teamwork can solve problems that seem impossible.
questions.hint: Read Priya's last realization.
questions.why: The last sentence names patience and teamwork as what solved the problem.

passages.title: Recycling Aluminum
passages.text: Aluminum cans can be recycled again and again without losing quality. Recycling a can uses about ninety-five percent less energy than making a new one from raw material. The process starts when a truck collects the cans, and a factory shreds and melts them. The melted metal is formed into sheets, which are then made into new cans. This entire cycle can take as little as sixty days. Because the metal is reused, fewer mines are needed, and less trash goes to landfills.

questions.q: How much less energy does recycling a can use than making a new one?
choices: About ninety-five percent less
About half as much energy
About the same amount of energy
questions.hint: Find the number in the second sentence.
questions.why: The text says recycling uses about ninety-five percent less energy.

questions.q: Why does recycling aluminum mean fewer mines are needed?
choices: Mines have already run out of aluminum.
The metal is reused, so less new metal is needed.
Factories now use only plastic for cans.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence. Look for "because".
questions.why: When metal is reused, there is less need to dig up new metal.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Aluminum is the strongest metal that people use every day.
Trucks collect aluminum cans from stores every sixty days.
Recycling aluminum cans saves energy and resources.
questions.hint: Choose the idea that covers all the details.
questions.why: The details about energy, mines, and landfills all show how recycling saves resources.

passages.title: Why Cities Build Green Roofs
passages.text: In crowded cities, rooftops are often bare surfaces of tar and gravel that absorb heat. On hot summer days, these dark roofs can become much warmer than the surrounding air, raising the temperature of the whole neighborhood. To address this problem, some architects design green roofs, which are rooftops covered with soil and plants. The vegetation shades the building and releases water vapor, which cools the air. A green roof also soaks up rainwater, reducing the amount that rushes into storm drains and floods streets. Although installing one costs more than a traditional roof, supporters argue that lower energy bills and a longer roof life eventually make up the difference.

questions.q: How do the plants on a green roof help cool the air?
choices: They shade the building and release water vapor.
They block the wind from the streets below.
They store heat to warm the building in winter.
questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins "The vegetation".
questions.why: The vegetation shades the building and releases water vapor, which cools the air.

questions.q: In this text, "vegetation" means...
choices: soil
plants
rainwater
questions.hint: The roof is covered with soil and plants. Which word names the living part?
questions.why: Vegetation means plants.

questions.q: Which statement is best supported by the text?
choices: Green roofs cost less than traditional roofs, even to install them.
Green roofs make the rain heavier in the city streets.
A green roof may cost less over time even though it costs more to install.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence, especially "Although" and "eventually".
questions.why: Supporters say savings eventually make up the higher installation cost.

passages.title: The Last Lighthouse Keeper
passages.text: For over forty years, Mr. Okafor climbed the spiral staircase of the Gull Point lighthouse each evening to light the great lamp. Ships depended on that beam to avoid the jagged rocks below. When automatic lights replaced human keepers, the harbor office announced that his services were no longer required. Mr. Okafor did not complain. On his final night, he polished the lens one last time and wrote in the logbook: "The light still turns." Years later, schoolchildren visiting the museum read the entry and understood that his work, though now done by machines, had once protected many lives.

questions.q: What replaced the human lighthouse keepers?
choices: Automatic lights
New ships
Museum guides
questions.hint: Read the sentence about what happened to the keepers' jobs.
questions.why: Automatic lights replaced human keepers.

questions.q: What does "The light still turns" suggest about Mr. Okafor?
choices: He was angry about losing the job he loved.
He was proud that the lighthouse would keep working.
He did not know that the lamp would be changed.
questions.hint: Think about how he behaved on his final night.
questions.why: He did not complain and polished the lens; the entry shows quiet pride.

questions.q: In this text, "depended on" means...
choices: argued with
wandered near
relied on
questions.hint: Ships needed the beam to avoid the rocks.
questions.why: If ships depended on the beam, they relied on it for safety.

passages.title: Learning a New Language
passages.text: Many adults believe that children learn languages effortlessly, but research suggests that the picture is more complicated. Young children do absorb sounds quickly, and they often develop native-like pronunciation. However, older learners usually have advantages of their own: they understand grammar rules, can use strategies for memorizing vocabulary, and know how to study. In one study, teenagers actually learned certain grammar patterns faster than younger children did. The best results appear to come from regular practice and many chances to use the language, no matter the learner's age.

questions.q: What advantages do older learners usually have?
choices: They understand grammar rules and know how to study.
They can copy the sounds of a new language more quickly.
They usually have much more free time in the day to practice.
questions.hint: Read the sentence that begins with "However".
questions.why: Older learners understand grammar rules, use strategies, and know how to study.

questions.q: Which sentence states the main idea best?
choices: Children are always better language learners than adults, so adults should not try.
Age matters, but regular practice and chances to use the language matter most.
Teenagers should avoid studying grammar rules and just listen.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence for the author's conclusion.
questions.why: The last sentence says the best results come from practice and chances to use the language.

questions.q: In this text, "effortlessly" means...
choices: with great care
in a very short time
without needing much effort
questions.hint: The adults believe learning is easy for children.
questions.why: Effortlessly means with little or no effort.

passages.title: Training the Immune System
passages.text: Your immune system protects the body from invaders such as bacteria and viruses. The first time it encounters a new germ, it needs several days to identify the threat and produce the right defenses, and during that delay a person can become seriously ill. A vaccine offers a safer way to gain that experience. It contains a harmless piece or weakened form of the germ, which is enough for the immune system to recognize it but not enough to cause the disease. The body responds by building antibodies and creating memory cells that remain for years. If the real germ ever appears, these memory cells launch a rapid response, often stopping the infection before symptoms begin. This is why vaccines are described as training rather than treatment.

questions.q: What do memory cells do?
choices: Launch a quick response when the real germ appears
Cause a mild form of the disease to start in the body
Destroy the vaccine after a few days inside the body
questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins "If the real germ ever appears".
questions.why: Memory cells launch a rapid response if the real germ appears.

questions.q: Why are vaccines described as training rather than treatment?
choices: They must be repeated every single day to keep working well.
They prepare the body before illness instead of curing an existing one.
They work only on germs that have already been weakened by the body.
questions.hint: Think about when a vaccine is given and what it does.
questions.why: A vaccine prepares the immune system ahead of time, like practice.

questions.q: In this text, "encounters" means...
choices: runs away from
gives to someone
comes across
questions.hint: The first time the immune system meets a new germ.
questions.why: To encounter something is to meet or come across it.

passages.title: The Extra Change
passages.text: Lucía had saved for months to buy her grandmother a scarf at the weekend market. When she arrived, however, she noticed that a vendor had mistakenly given her extra change, enough to buy a second scarf. Her first instinct was to walk away quietly; after all, no one had noticed. Yet the vendor, an older woman with tired eyes, was counting her coins nervously as customers drifted past. Lucía hesitated, then returned the money. The vendor's face softened. "Not everyone would have come back," she said. Lucía shrugged, but as she carried the scarf home she felt lighter than she had all week.

questions.q: Why did Lucía feel "lighter" on the way home?
choices: She felt good about doing the honest thing.
The scarf was very light to carry.
She had spent less money than she planned.
questions.hint: Think about what she did with the extra change.
questions.why: "Lighter" is figurative: returning the money lifted her worry.

questions.q: In this text, "hesitated" means...
choices: moved quickly without thinking
paused because she was unsure
became very angry
questions.hint: She had an instinct to walk away, but she did something else.
questions.why: Hesitating means pausing before you act.

questions.q: Which detail suggests the vendor needed the money?
choices: She sold scarves at a weekend market.
She thanked Lucía with a smile.
She counted her coins nervously.
questions.hint: Look at how the vendor is described before Lucía returns the money.
questions.why: Nervous coin counting and tired eyes suggest she could not afford the loss.

passages.title: How Sound Travels
passages.text: Sound is created when an object vibrates, causing the surrounding air particles to bump into one another in a chain reaction. This wave of vibrations travels outward until it reaches your ear, where tiny structures translate it into signals your brain can interpret. Because sound depends on particles to carry it, it cannot travel through empty space. Interestingly, it moves faster through water than through air, and faster still through steel, because particles in denser materials are packed closer together and pass vibrations along more quickly. This explains why a person who puts an ear against a railroad track can detect an approaching train long before it can be heard through the air.

questions.q: Why can sound not travel through empty space?
choices: It needs particles to carry its vibrations.
It becomes too quiet for anyone to measure.
It is absorbed by the sun's strong light.
questions.hint: Find the sentence that begins with "Because".
questions.why: Sound depends on particles to carry it, and empty space has none.

questions.q: Why might a person hear a train through a track before hearing it through the air?
choices: Trains are much louder when they are on the ground.
Sound moves faster through steel than through air.
Air blocks the vibrations from moving at all.
questions.hint: Use the sentence about water, air, and steel.
questions.why: Sound travels faster through denser materials such as steel.

questions.q: What does this text mainly explain?
choices: How the human ear is built and how each part of it works.
Why trains make such loud noises when they move along tracks.
How sound is made and why its speed depends on the material it moves through.
questions.hint: Choose the answer that covers the whole text.
questions.why: It explains how sound begins, travels, and changes speed in different materials.
